newsitem.title: USA: CCB becomes bigger takeover target-analysts.
newsitem.headline: CCB becomes bigger takeover target-analysts.

text.p: CCB Financial Corp raised its own profile as a takeover target on Tuesday when it announced it would acquire American Federal Bank FSB, analysts said.

While the acquisition would boost CCB's assets and deposits as well as give it a new robust market in neighboring South Carolina, where American Federal is based, CCB remains just one of three mid-tier banks based in North Carolina.
"Anyone looking at a takeover would look at them (CCB) even greater," said Davenport & Co analyst David West.
Added John Coffey of Robinson-Humphrey: "In the food chain of banking, CCB just got more attractive."
After announcement of the $325.1-million proposed merger, CCB's shares were off 2-1/8 to 65-7/8 while American Federal rose six to 27-1/2.
First Citizens BancShares Inc and Centura Banks are the other mid-sized publicly-traded banks in the state.
Midsized banks cannot match the product and service offerings of larger banks, such as vast automated teller machine networks or banking by computer.
The deal would expand the CCB franchise from its base in Durham, N.C., and down the Interstate-85 corridor that runs through South Carolina's dynamic markets.
"They were relatively small but located in a good market, so they were on a lot of people's radar screens," West said of American Federal, a $1.3 billion thrift in Greenville, S.C.
The U.S. arm of German carmaker Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG is in the market, along with French tiremaker Michelin SA, Flagstar Cos Inc and many others.
CCB spokesman John Ramsey called the shift into South Carolina a "natural extension" even though the goal was not to reach into the deep pockets of big business.

"We're primarily a consumer and small business bank, as is American Federal," Ramsey said. "While those (big) businesses are growing, people are moving in; and big businesses spawn a whole host of smaller businesses, and as those markets expand we have opportunities there too."
Coffey questioned the $325.1 million in stock, or $28.86 per share, price that CCB offered for American Federal but said strategically the two institutions make a good fit.
"The price looks high but American Federal is not an ordinary thrift," Coffey said. "It's a bank-like company and is getting a bank-like price."

The deal "looks neutral to slightly additive to their (CCB's) earnings," he added. After the transaction, CCB would have assets of about $6.90 billion, up from $5.54 billion in the fourth quarter a year ago. Deposits would increase to $5.72 billion from $4.73 billion.
The deal is expected to close by the third quarter.
Ernest Roessler, 55, would remain chairman, president and cheif executive of CCB.
Roy Abercrombie, 49, president and chief executive of American Federal, would become CCB vice chairman.
Three members of American Federal's board of directors would also be added to the CCB board for a total of 23 members.
The merger is subject to due diligence, shareholder and regulatory approvals.
CCB currently operates 161 banking offices throughout North Carolina, while American Federal operates 40 banking offices throughout northwest South Carolina.
